items.title: Big Sugar Gravel: Kongstad and Hobbs Claim the Final Gravel Crowns of the Year
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: Keegan Swenson and Sofia Gomez Villafañe took the overall Life Time Grand Prix series wins.
items.lbText:
Tobias Kongstad and Stella Hobbs took wins at the 2026 Life Time Grand Prix after two fast-paced races over the rough-and-tumble Northwest Arkansas gravel.

Kongstad, who is the team manager and top male rider for the PAS Normal gravel team, took the win from a nine-man sprint after benefiting from the Life Time Grand Prix series battles between his rivals. Henry Nelson came close to stealing the show with a late solo breakaway, but he was caught in the final paved run-in back to Bentonville.

Martins Blums finished second in the sprint while Cole Paton finished third.

In the women’s race, Hobbs made a similar move to Nelson, but she managed to quickly pull out a gap of over a minute. While it was a big chase group behind, Hobbs managed to pull out enough of a gap to survive the charge from behind with time to spare.

Sofia Gomez Villafañe won the sprint for second ahead of Hayley Preen. Third was enough for Villafañe to wrap up another Life Time Grand Prix overall title, with Preen finishing second in the standings.

items.title: EF Cycling Team Parodies Ferrari F1 ‘Unofficial Statement’ Prank in Aftermath of Carapaz Shock Exit
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: EF Education-EasyPost fights for control of the narrative by mimicking Ferrari's viral Hamilton and Leclerc 'highjack' post.
items.lbText:
EF Education-EasyPost parodied the viral “Unofficial Statement” social media post made last week by the Scuderia Ferrari Formula 1 team.

At face value, it’s a smart social media tactic to build hype around news of new rider signings.

Below that, the skeptics might say it’s an even smarter PR move to take control of the narrative.

On Friday, marquee rider Richard Carapaz stunned the cycling world and sparked speculation when he broke contract with the team to sign with WorldTour rivals, NSN Cycling.

In its Instagram post on Saturday, EF Education-EasyPost suggested Ben Healy and Sean Quinn “hacked” its social media channels and posted untimely information regarding the 2027 roster. Velo is not aware of any anomalous posts made to the team’s account.

Slide one of the post is an “Unofficial Statement.”

Slide two features Healy and Quinn looking “mischievous.”

The American team’s post is a carbon copy of one made by Scuderia Ferrari at the start of this month.

The Formula 1 powerhouse posted an online “Unofficial Statement” after Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc “hijacked” the team’s social media channels. The two superstar drivers had posted a series of bizarre selfies and prank reels to the team’s accounts in the preceding hours.

The Scuderia Ferrari “statement” soon racked up more than two million “likes” and 14,000 comments on Instagram.

“EF Pro Cycling confirms that earlier this week, two individuals within the organization gained unauthorized access to our social media channels.

“During this period, a series of highly questionable editorial decisions were made, including the premature distribution of confidential information regarding our 2027 rider roster. We ask that anyone who received these communications disregard them immediately and refrain from sharing any information until the official announcements begin on October 19.

“We can now confirm that the two suspects have been identified and the situation is now under control.

“We thank our fans for their patience and understanding during this unprecedented incident.”

The Scuderia Ferrari post is at the bottom of this page.

It’s not unusual for teams to build hype for new rider announcements and kit reveals. This prank is well in-line with EF Education-EasyPost’s forward-thinking, unconventional ethos.

We can now expect Jonathan Vaughers’ team to reveal some new signings this coming Monday, October 19.

On Friday, Carapaz broke his ongoing contract for a landmark three-year deal with the budding NSN Cycling Team.

The news blows a huge hole in EF Education-EasyPost.

This year alone, the Ecuadorian finished top-10 at the Tour de France and Vuelta a España, and won two Tour stages. He was by far the squad’s highest-ranked, most recognizable rider.

Carapaz’s exit lit up social media Friday and ignited speculation about EF Education-EasyPost’s future.

The 33-year-old was the seventh rider to confirm they’re leaving the team this winter. Meanwhile, the squad has named only one signing for 2027 – Gavin Sherry, who is promoted from the EF Education-Aevolo devo team.

On Saturday, FE Education-EasyPost attempted to shift the vibes.

items.title: Sean Kelly: Here’s Why Pogačar Doesn’t Have to Fear Seixas Anytime Soon
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Paul Seixas ended his season with a stunning Il Lombardia win, yet Kelly feels Tadej Pogačar’s reign is secure. For now at least.
items.lbText:
Paul Seixas is seen as a likely successor to Tadej Pogačar. (Photo: Maarten Straetemans / Belga / AFP) (Photo: MAARTEN STRAETEMANS)

Paul Seixas has made remarkable progress this season, notching up eight wins in all, including a Tadej Pogačar -type dominance of Il Lombardia last weekend.

However although Seixas’ Cannibalesque ascent of the Civiglio saw him break the record Pogačar set four years ago on the same climb, and despite a stunning rate of improvement this season, experienced cycling analyst Sean Kelly feels the world number one shouldn’t lose sleep anytime soon.

Kelly spoke to Velo this week about the two riders and explained why he is believes Pogačar will have the edge for some time yet.

“If you had Pogačar there on Saturday, Seixas probably would have been able to stay with him once again,” he said, speaking of the hilly finale of Il Lombardia. “But then in the flat sprint he doesn’t have any chance, because Pogačar is very fast in a two-up sprint or a little group sprint.

“It’s the other quality that he’s got. As I said many times, Pogačar can do fecking everything.”

Seixas turned heads in Liège-Bastogne-Liège when the then 19-year-old was the only rider able to hold onto Pogačar when the UAE Emirates-XRG rider went all out on La Redoute.

He stayed with him to the summit and then began trading pulls with him afterward. The duo continued together out front until the defending champion put in a last-gasp surge on the climb of La Roche aux Faucons. That finally broke Seixas, but Pogačar admitted afterward that he had believed they’d reach the finish line together.

It’s incredibly rare for any rider to be able to cling on when Pogačar is going all out on a tough climb. It was an even more remarkable achievement for a 19-year-old second-year professional, and it highlighted the extraordinary talent the Frenchman has.

But Kelly insists that even if Seixas is able to remain with Pogačar, that’s only one part of the game.

“There’s no weakness with him where you can say, ‘oh yeah, we can get him on that one.’ They’re just not there. So I don’t think Pogačar is going to be worried.”

There will be some who will disagree with Kelly’s point. They will point to the large age gap between the two riders, a full eight years. They will note that Pogačar has just turned 28, an age when riders are in their prime, and note that it’s very often the time where performances start to plateau and then, a year or two later, start to decline.

Still, Kelly doesn’t think that will be an issue anytime soon. He argues Pogačar will remain the best rider in the sport as long as one thing is in place: motivation.

“Pogačar at 28, 29 or 30 – if mentally he’s hungry enough to do it, I don’t think there’s going to be a problem age-wise,” the former world number one said. “Pogačar definitely has another three or four top years left in him. But will he do four years? Will he have that focus, the mentality to continue on?

“We hear about these long term contracts and that, but in three years’ time, if Pogačar said after the Tour de France, ‘I’m finished, that’s it, I’m stopping at the end of this year,’ it wouldn’t surprise me.”

Pogačar’s ability to stay at the top level is one vital element in any speculation about their future tussles.

The other relates to the Frenchman himself. Kelly acknowledged that Seixas is forging new ground, being the youngest-ever winner of Il Lombardia, and also becoming the youngest rider to start the Tour de France in 89 years.

Those kinds of performances, plus Seixas’ stunning rate of improvement this year—remember, he had no pro wins at all prior to 2025, and now he has eight—lead many to assume that he will leap up another level in 2027.

Hold on, says Kelly. It’s not necessarily accurate to make such presumptions.

“It depends now where Seixas goes from here,” he explained. “Will he continue on improving? Is there much more improvement left in him? Or is he a very early developer, and the level he’s at now is pretty much the level he’s going to be at?

“Maybe that is going to be his best level.”

It seems unlikely that a talented young rider could stop improving, but Kelly believes an error was made this year. He explains what that was and how he thinks it might affect cycling’s most exciting young rider.

“I would be concerned that it was too young to do a Tour de France this year,” he said. “And also to ride it as he did, going for the general classification, every day being there in the battle. His potential might suffer because of doing the Tour de France too young.

“I would be concerned that a guy at 19, doing a Tour of France [as intensely] as they do it now, it could affect his performance next year, the year after. He mightn’t get that potential that would be there if he had been taken along at an easier level.”

Kelly mentions Laurent Fignon as a rider from his era who was incredibly good very young. The Frenchman won the Tour at 22 and 23 but, despite those incredible early performances, never won the race again. He missed out by eight seconds to Greg LeMond in 1989 and won the Giro that same year, but it’s fair to say that his early momentum didn’t lead to the dominance many had predicted.

To be clear, Kelly is wowed by Seixas. He does suggest that slightly sub-par performances by Isaac del Toro and Remco Evenepoel in Il Lombardia made the Frenchman look even better than he was but, nevertheless, he applauds his performance.

He also gives credit where credit is due for the year as a whole.

“You couldn’t but be impressed about the performances. We were hearing about the power outputs that he was doing in training,” he said. “We were hearing all that and then he comes to Pays Basques, the way he dominated there.

“The way he dominated the beginning of the year, that confirmed what we were hearing, what the French were talking him up about. And he’s confirmed all that through the year.…

items.title: The Best Pro Cyclists’ FTPs Are Even Higher Than You Thought
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: We compare the FTPs of Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, and more.
items.lbText:
When Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney won atop Mont Ventoux in the Tour de France Femmes this summer, we thought it was one of the best climbing performances in cycling history . Since then, more information has come out, not only confirming Niewiadoma-Phinney’s performance, but putting it on the pedestal as the greatest climb in the history of women’s cycling.

We estimated Niewiadoma-Phinney’s output at 5.3w/kg for the duration of Mont Ventoux. But in a social media post, Niewiadoma-Phinney’s husband, Taylor, said that the actual output was closer to 5.6w/kg. This is due to the fact that Niewiadoma-Phinney rode into a headwind in the final third of the climb, and that her raw power output is relatively low, making her power-to-weight ratio even higher.

Niewiadoma-Phinney is one of a small group of riders in the women’s pro peloton who can probably hold 6w/kg for 10-20 minutes. These types of numbers were unfathomable a few years ago, but just like the men’s side of the sport, we have seen professional cycling progressing at a rapid rate. Niewiadoma-Phinney’s performance on Mont Ventoux was one of those moments where we had to rewrite the power curve for women’s cycling. If you could hold 5w/kg for an hour in 2025, you could fight for the podium at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift. But in 2026, 5w/kg won’t even put you in the top five.

In this article, we’ll lay out the best women’s riders’ FTPs, and explain why it is their strength or weakness. Let’s start with none other than the Tour de France Femmes and world championship winner.

The last time that Demi Vollering posted power data publicly was in 2022, but her file from the 2021 Liège-Bastogne-Liège Femmes is still on Strava. The Dutchwoman pushed 362w (6.3w/kg) for 4min 34sec on La Redoute, and went on to take the win in a small group sprint. Since then, Vollering’s power data has disappeared, but we can make some educated guesses as to how much she’s improved.

Vollering finished second on Mont Ventoux, 1:16 behind Niewiadoma-Phinney in the queen stage of the TDFF. But she had attacked on the bottom slopes of the climb, pushing the pace and inadvertently setting up a perfect counterattack for Niewiadoma-Phinney. Vollering and Marlen Reusser were nearly two minutes behind Niewiadoma-Phinney with a few kilometers to go, but then Vollering put in a massive attack to close the gap by more than 30 seconds. That kind of acceleration is only possible when you’ve been riding well under threshold, suggesting that Vollering had plenty left in the tank while Niewiadoma-Phinney rode away solo.

Despite only pushing an estimated 5.1w/kg for the majority of Mont Ventoux, Vollering finished with such a burst that her actual FTP must be significantly higher. Based on our calculations, Vollering has an FTP of just over 300w, putting her at 5.3w/kg at an estimated weight of 57kg. That means that Vollering has a fantastic balance between raw power and w/kg. It’s why she can drop most riders on a climb, but she can also drop them on a shallow descent. She can solo to victory on the flats, and win a small group sprint with her raw power output. For her biggest rival at this year’s Tour de France Femmes, it is a completely different story.

At an estimated 49kg, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney is about 8kg lighter than Vollering, and more than 20kg lighter than Marlen Reusser. That creates a massive raw power discrepancy between the rivals, with few scenarios in Niewiadoma-Phinney’s favor. One of the only times that Niewiadoma-Phinney has the upper hand is on steep climbs. We saw this at the TDFF, when Niewiadoma-Phinney broke away on Mont Ventoux, and was able to follow Vollering’s attacks on a number of short and punchy climbs.

But as soon as they reach the descent or flat section of road, Niewiadoma-Phinney is immediately disadvantaged. We saw this clearly on stages 8 and 9 of this year’s Tour de France Femmes. Niewiadoma-Phinney was only a few seconds behind Vollering at the crest of a key climb, but then she would lose 20-30 seconds on the descent. These were shallow, non-technical descents of 3-5%, meaning that raw power and high speed would dominate.

But on the long and steep climb to Mont Ventoux, Niewiadoma-Phinney’s power-to-weight ratio reigned supreme. The Pole broke away on the steepest section of the climb, building an insurmountable lead before the shallower and windier section of the course. At 49kg, she was giving away 50-100w compared to Vollering and Reusser, but that didn’t matter on a 9% gradient.

Niewiadoma-Phinney likely has the highest FTP in terms of watts per kilogram in women’s cycling. She reportedly did 5.6w/kg for 55 minutes on Mont Ventoux, which means her fresh numbers could be even higher.

Niewiadoma-Phinney – Mont Ventoux (UPDATED)

Steep Section to Chalet Reynard : 32:09 at 5.7w/kg (1,540 Vm/h)

In stark contrast to Niewiadoma-Phinney’s power-to-weight ratio is Marlen Reusser, one of the tallest and most powerful women in professional cycling. Standing at 1.8 meters tall, the Swiss rider weighs an estimated 70kg, meaning that she has more raw power than perhaps any other woman in the world. In fact, her estimated FTP of 370w is world class, regardless of gender.

Reusser was in the shape of her life at this year’s Tour de France Femmes, and she was riding into a podium spot before a final stage collapse in Nice. But before that, Reusser was following Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney on every piece of terrain. Short climbs, long climbs, technical descents, flats, and final sprints…Reusser was there every step of the way. She even won the 21-kilometer time trial in Dijon, putting 18 seconds into Vollering and over a minute into Niewiadoma-Phinney.…

items.title: I Tested Infinit Nutrition in Death Valley. It’s Worth Full Price.
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: I usually wait for a discount to highlight gear, but after two brutal 10-hour days in Death Valley, Infinit’s Custom Mix proved it is worth every penny of full retail.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

My big-ride nutrition strategy is constantly evolving, but when I headed to Death Valley for three 12-hour days on the bike (which turned into two 10-hours days because we were fast then there was a hurricane), I packed a bag of Infinit Nutrition. Sitting at my desk with the trip behind me, I can call it a success. That desert loop was the toughest ride I can remember from a fueling perspective, making Infinit worth putting back on your radar. If you struggle with nutrition on massive days, this could be the answer.

What makes Infinit unique is the custom blend. If you want to get highly specific, you can use a Nix Hydration sensor to measure your sweat composition and use that data to place your order. (I previously wrote a deep dive on pairing the Nix sensor with Infinit if you want the full process). You don’t have to get that technical though. Instead answering a few straight forward questions on the website is enough to build your mix.

For me, the biggest advantage is the sodium control. I prefer to drink my calories rather than eat them, and as a salty sweater, I need serious salt replacement. On long endurance rides, if the sodium ratio is off, I end up desperately thirsty no matter how much water I take in. Infinit allows me to dial in the exact amount of sodium, add a bit of protein, and keep everything easy on the stomach for all-day drinking.

items.title: Driver Who Killed Cyclist Magnus White Denied Parole
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: Yeva Smilianska has served a little more than one year of a four-year sentence. She is next eligible for parole in one year.
items.lbText:
Yeva Smilianska, the driver convicted last year of hitting and killing Magnus White , 17, was denied parole yesterday. It was her first opportunity for parole after serving a little more than one year of a four-year sentence.

Smilianska was convicted in June 2025 of reckless vehicular homicide for striking and killing White outside Boulder, Colorado in late July 2023. White, a rising star in the USA Cycling program, had been out on a training ride shortly before he was scheduled to head off to Europe for a block of racing.

The White family believes that had Smilianska been drug tested at the scene, she would have faced a more severe punishment than the four-year sentence she ultimately received.

Smilianska maintained that she was tired after hanging out with friends and called her decision to get behind the wheel “horribly irresponsible” in the parole hearing. She maintains that she only drank a small amount that evening, and did not address evidence from the trial showing that she had been drinking before getting behind the wheel.

Smilianska addressed how her actions have impacted Magnus’ family, though did not mention Magnus’ name, saying “I can’t imagine how they handle all this. I know there’s nothing I can do or say anything. If there were, I would happily do it.”

“I wish I could do anything to help the damage I caused.”

Michael White, Magnus’ father, shared an Instagram post detailing the process of what it was like to listen in on the parole hearing as a family.

“This is what a parole hearing looks like,” he wrote.

“We’re not in a courtroom. We’re not at a prison. We’re in our living room. We haven’t showered. We sit as family, even our dog, and we wait for them to call us.

“At today’s hearing, we heard her speak for the first time ever in a casual, conversational setting. That’s how the interview goes with a parole board member. She didn’t know we were listening in on the hearing. It’s our right as victims.

“After listening to everything she said, it’s clear she STILL doesn’t take responsibility for killing Magnus. She told the parole board member, ‘I was hanging out with a friend, then the car crash happened.’ Then she blamed Magnus’ death on not getting ‘extra sleep.’

“When she was asked about the impact on the victim’s family, she started talking about herself. ‘I’m really struggling about what happened to myself.’ She never said Magnus’ name the entire hearing.”

He went on to thank everyone who wrote an impact statement before the hearing, saying that the Department of Corrections told them the over 500 letters was by far the most they had ever received.

“Today, we can breathe again,” White wrote.

Smilianska is eligible to seek parole again in one year.

The White family started the White Line Foundation with the goal of ending vulnerable road user deaths. Learn more and donate at thewhiteline.org

items.title: Richard Carapaz Breaks Contract with EF Education-EasyPost to Join NSN in Transfer Stunner
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Carapaz and NSN Cycling Team confirm three-year deal that leaves a void at EF and will reshape grand tour racing in 2027.
items.lbText:
Richard Carapaz has split from EF Education-EasyPost to join NSN Cycling Team on a three-year deal that will see him toward retirement.

The bombshell transfer was confirmed Friday afternoon after a wave of speculation following recent reports by Wielerflits .

The 33-year-old had an ongoing contract with the American EF Education-EasyPost team and had enjoyed a wildly successful 2026 season.

He finished top-10 at both the Tour de France and Vuelta a España, and claimed the Tour de France KoM jersey for a second time.

According to Wielerflits , EF Education-EasyPost is suffering a budget pinch going into 2027. The Ecuadorian would have been one of the highest-paid riders on the roster of Jonathan Vaughters’ team.

Carapaz’s exit will be hard felt at EF. He’s been the center of the squad’s ambitions for the past four seasons.

Beyond that, the U.S. team was already reeling from a rider exodus. Five others, including classics talent Kasper Asgreen, have recently confirmed they’re leaving this winter. Asgreen also joins NSN Cycling Team in 2027.

Meanwhile, EF Education-EasyPost has confirmed only one incoming transfer for 2027. Young American Gavin Sherry steps up from the EF-Aevolo devo team.

“Gracias, Richie. Por todo,” EF wrote in a montage video of Carapaz’s greatest hits it posted to Instagram .

NSN Cycling Team heralded Carapaz’s arrival Friday as “a major statement that will strengthen the roster and the team’s grand tour and stage race ambitions.”

The former Giro d’Italia winner and Olympic champion will join Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt in a new climbing division of the Swiss-registered squad.

Having only formed out of the ashes of Israel Premier-Tech at the start of 2026, NSN was focused on sprints with Biniam Girmay and Ethan Vernon in its debut season.

“For me, it’s a tremendous opportunity as a rider to be part of this project and, above all, to be one of the team’s leaders,” Carapaz said Friday.

“I find the NSN project really interesting. After our first conversations, I was convinced this would be the right place for me. I’m a rider who has achieved great results throughout my career, many of which were in the grand tours, and that fits very well with what NSN was looking for,” Carapaz continued.

“The team has big ambitions to keep growing and already in my conversations with the performance team, it was clear we share the same desire to keep improving and achieve big things together.”

items.title: VIDEO: Mass Crash Decimates Women’s Omnium at UCI Track World Championships
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Lorena Wiebes forced to abandon her Omnium title defense Friday at UCI track worlds after being at the center of huge pileup.
items.lbText:
Lorena Wiebes was taken out of her Omnium world title defense by a shocking mass crash Friday at the UCI track world championships.

The Dutch rider was one of 13 to fall in the 24-rider scratch race, the opening round of the multi-format Omnium event.

Wiebes had started the Omnium world championships as both the favorite and defending champion.

She was ultimately the one woman who had to pull out after the high-speed pileup Friday on the steep banking of the corner of the Shanghai velodrome.

Video from the race broadcast reveals Wiebes was one of the first to come down after she was squeezed between two rival riders.

The 27-year-old landed hard on her right shoulder before a mass of bodies and bikes came over her.

Wiebes was able to stagger away with help from her Dutch team staff but was clearly dazed and heavily banged up.

La montonera en el scratch del ómnium en la que Lorena Wiebes es de las más afectadas y no podrá defender su 🌈 #Shanghai2026 pic.twitter.com/hLjQtahSr0

Fortunately, the damage might have been limited. Wiebes later reappeared to the trackside, albeit shrouded in medical dressing and gauze.

Meanwhile, emergency services were quick on the scene to support the other riders who fell. The race was restarted around 15 minutes later.

Japanese racer Tsuyaka Uchino won the round.

Wiebes will no doubt be wondering “what if” in the aftermath of the crash.

The SD-Worx Protime racer was unstoppable all through her road season. She came into track worlds red hot after winning all three stages and the GC at the Tour of Chongming Island WorldTour race last week.

The UCI track world championships in Shanghai, China, run through Sunday, October 18.

items.title: Roglič, Carapaz, Bernal: Retirement Talk and Bombshell Rumors Leave Questions over 3 Grand Tour Greats
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Carapaz reported to be splitting from EF to join NSN in move that would reshape the narrative as Rogič and Bernal address retirement rumors.
items.lbText:
Primoz Roglič , Egan Bernal , Richard Carapaz – rewind to before Tadej Pogačar changed everything, and they were the men to beat.

These three grand tour champions now face uncertain or wildly intriguing futures.

Mountains king and GC threat Carapaz is reportedly due to split from EF Education-EasyPost to join the upstart NSN Cycling Team.

Roglič is being as elusive as ever about his future. We still don’t know whether we’ll see the four-time Vuelta a España winner and Slovenian OG race again.

And Bernal? He’s batted away rumors that he’s going to retire, but he sounded far from convinced.

It could be all-change for three superstars who drove the narrative of the pre-Pogačar era.

Sure, they’re not grand tour favorites any longer, but they continue to influence every race they show up to. What they do next will alter the texture of the sport.

Richard Carapaz is reportedly poised to break his ongoing contract with EF Education-EasyPost to join NSN Cycling Team.

If it happens, it would be the biggest signing of the season, by far.

Rumors have been swirling for some time that Carapaz was considering an early exit from the American EF team. NSN, Netcompany Ineos, and Pinarello-Q36.5 were touted as possible new employers.

Wielerflits reported Friday that NSN Cycling Team – the squad that formed last year out of the ashes of Israel-Premier Tech – won the battle for the Ecuadorian star’s contract. The move has not yet been confirmed.

If it happens, it’s definitely not a transfer we had on our bingo card.

Carapaz has a long leash at EF Education-EasyPost. The 33-year-old chases stages or GC as he pleases. He seems to thrive in the American team’s all-attacking, always-the-underdog environment.

His palmarés from 2026 proves that point. Two stage wins and the polka dot jersey at the Tour de France, and fourth at the Vuelta? Carapaz is doing just fine .

However, according to Wielerflits , Jonathan Vaughters’ team is suffering a budget pinch. Carapaz would be gobbling a huge chunk of the team’s payroll.

Carapaz would change the identity of team NSN in 2027 if Wielerflits’ reporting is true.

Having already signed Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt, amongst others, the peloton would have a dangerous new climbing team.

What’s going on with Primož Roglič? Nobody knows, and he’s hardly dropping any clues either.

The Slovenian star raced for the last time with Red Bull Bora-Hansgrohe last weekend at Il Lombardia, and has nothing confirmed for 2027.

But old dog Rog clearly has more to give.

Victory at the European time trial championships, a swashbuckling ride at the road world championships, and second overall at the Vuelta a España put an exclamation point on the 36-year-old’s season.

After initial reports that Rogla would race on with the Belgian Lotto-Intermarché team in 2027, Tudor Pro Cycling and Pinarello-Q36.5 are now reportedly also in the hunt for his signature.

Speaking at Il Lombardia last Saturday, Roglič was characteristically cryptic about his future.

“You never know when it is the last [race],” he said.

When asked if he will continue to race next year, he said, “I don’t know yet. We will see. We will see.”

Tudor Pro Cycling and Pinarello-Q36.5 have both been busy on the transfer market this season. Roglič would be a prize addition for either of these rival ProTeams.

Pinarello-Q36.5 in particular has been making waves in this “silly season.” The squad is plundering billionaire backer Ivan Glasenberg’s deep pockets to build a superteam around Tom Pidcock.

Giulio Ciccone and Mauro Schmid headline 11 new signings for the 2027 season. If Roglič is poised to be number 12, he’s not dropping any clues about it.

Egan Bernal to retire aged 29? It was a rumor that rocked the cycling world last week.

According to reporting by contract sleuth Daniel Benson , the former Tour de France and Giro d’Italia winner was contemplating hanging up his wheels for good.

Bernal took only some of the heat out of the speculation last week when he responded with a lengthy Instagram message. The tone was far from conclusive.

“I have a contract with the team through 2029, and for now, my intention is to start next season,” Bernal wrote on Instagram.

Bernal hasn’t raced since the Tour de France. He wrote that after a busy early-season, he had needed time off the grid in summer to reflect on his future.

His statement leaves questions over how long “Bernalito” may remain a pro bike racer.

“I decided to end my season after the Tour de France this year. I needed some time for myself – to rest, relax a little, and regain the peace that can sometimes be lost amidst the pace of racing,” Bernal wrote.

“I want to give myself the time and space needed to face what lies ahead with the same conviction and dedication I have always had,” he continued. “I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now. For now, I want to enjoy the present, experience this moment calmly, and let time take its course.”

Bernal seems at a crossroads in his career, right when it was regaining momentum.

The Colombian star was set back by more than a year after he suffered a terrifying, life-threatening crash into the back of a bus in winter 2022.

Finishing seventh at the Giro d’Italia and winning a stage at the Vuelta a España last summer suggested maybe, say it quietly, “ Bernal’s bac k.” Fifth at Liège-Bastogne-Liège and 10th at this year’s Giro d’Italia reinforced murmurs of a return to form.

Bernal has three more years on his contract with Netcompany Ineos. How many of those he completes seems very uncertain right now.
