items.title: Stress Testing 6 Completely Different Gravel Bikes to Find the Future of Gravel
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: In episode 2 of the Velo Gravel Field Test, we put our 6 test bikes through 3 rounds of head to head challenges: climbing, descending, and efficiency.
items.lbText:
What does the future of gravel bikes look like? That’s the question we’re exploring in Velo’s 2027 Gravel Bike Field Test .

From aero bikes with extra tire clearance to what can only be classified as a mountain bike with drop bars, there are more approaches than ever to gravel bikes. We’ve curated a selection of six examples of modern gravel bikes, each progressive in its own way, and put them head to head in Squamish, B.C. to see where exactly gravel is headed.

Last week in episode 1 , we took our six test bikes on a first impressions loop that featured a little bit of everything: champagne gravel, loamy dirt trails, and slightly technical, rocky single track—with climbing and descending for all of the above.

Now Levy, Josh, and Logan are back for episode 2, where it’s time to put each bike through a series of challenges designed to push the bikes (and, frankly, the test riders) to their limits to see how well they perform under the wide range of different conditions that can all be called gravel riding.

Logan drew the short straw this time around, picking the climbing challenge—but he doesn’t seem too bummed about it. Can somebody please stop making him call it interval training? How does each bike handle an off-road climb sprinkled with a few challenging elements like rocks and roots? We timed each run to find out.

Next up, it’s Levy’s turn, and he’s drawing on his 20+ years of mountain biking experience in the descending challenge. This technical singletrack is definitely on the outer limits of where you’d want to take a gravel bike, but that’s the point of the challenge—pushing these bikes to their limits.

No one on the Velo tech team likes to ride long distances quite like Josh, who’s known to do at least one century ride every week, so naturally he’s taken on our efficiency test. We had him ride every bike on a washboard gravel road while holding a steady 200 watts to see which of our six bikes comes out on top.

The all-rounder: race it or go adventuring.

Specification: Giant Revolt Advanced SL 0, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed: 53mm Weight (tested size): 7.85kg/17.3lbs (ML)

Specification : Factor Sarana, SRAM Force XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 9.58kg/21.12lbs (Medium)

Specification : Argon 18 Anti Matter + SRAM RED XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 55mm Weight (tested size) : 8.5kg/18.74lbs (Medium)

Specification : Obed GVR, SRAM Red XPLR Tire clearance, claimed : 56mm Weight (tested size) : 9.12kg/20.1lbs (Medium)

Specification : Pivot Les SL Drop Bar, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission 12-Speed Tire clearance, claimed : 29 x 2.4″ Weight (tested size) : 9.78kg/21.56lbs (Medium)

The 32er. How much difference do big wheels make?

Specification : Salsa Fargo 32 Ti, SRAM GX Eagle Transmission Tire clearance, claimed : 60mm Weight (tested size) : 9.48kg/20.9lbs (Medium)

To settle the debate about the future of gravel once and for all (or perhaps muddy it more than ever), we’ve assembled three test riders who, like the bikes, couldn’t be more different.

Reformed mountain biker turned drop-bar obsessive Mike Levy leads the charge, bringing a technical, rowdy background and a preference for chunkier roads and adventuring far off the beaten path—on Earth and beyond.

He’s joined by Velo’s in-house team of tech editors. Josh Ross likes to ride long distances as efficiently as possible—catch him pedaling all day and night across the gravel roads of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. He’s all about pushing his personal boundaries, and finding the equipment that will help him go the extra mile (or extra 200 miles).

Having once finished 18th overall at the Unbound 200, Logan Jones-Wilkins can’t stop thinking about going fast and squeezing every drop of performance from gravel gear. But when he’s not mixing it up in the pointy end of races, he likes his gravel bike to be a medium for adventuring into the unknown.

That’s three different approaches to gravel, and, naturally, their takes are as varied as the riders themselves. Can they settle their differences and agree on anything? We may have to resort to some good ol’ fashioned tactics to resolve things—which may or may not mean go-kart racing.

To put these bikes to the ultimate test (and the riders too), we’ve taken everyone to the outdoor playground that is Squamish, British Columbia. Finding out the future of gravel means pushing bikes to their limits, so we’ve found a mix of terrain from single track to washboard fire roads to do just that.

We’re stress testing the bikes to get the most possible out of them. In this first episode, we’ve put together a test loop that takes our riders on a smattering of every kind of terrain one might consider gravel, from champagne roads, to loamy dirt trails, to slightly technical, rocky single track, and we’ve got climbing and descending for all of the above.

To keep our testing focused on the bikes themselves, we’ve brought in control tires, 50mm Schwalbe G-One RX tires run at the same tire pressure, mounted to Easton EC90 ALX wheels .

Velo Field Test wouldn’t happen without the support of these sponsors. A big thank you to Endura for providing kits and helmets, Schwalbe for tires, and Easton for wheels!

A special thank you to the crew who made this Velo Field Test a reality!

Enjoy the video and stay tuned for episode 3, where we’re taking the bikes on a big ride around Squamish to figure out the future of gravel bikes.

items.title: Moots Launches the County Line — an All-Road Bike Fit for SBT
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The new offering from the Steamboat Springs-based brand brings an all-rounder with 42mm of clearance to its titanium range of drop-bar bikes.
items.lbText:
The all new County Line all-road bike from Moots. (Photo: Moots)

Moots has entered the all-road game with its County Line frame, a bike built to offer more traction, stability, and control than a conventional road bike. The brand that specializes in titanium frames launched its new bike as a true all-round option, optimized around 38mm tires with clearance up to 42mm.

Like all Moots frames, the County Line is manufactured in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, and is built to reflect certain aspects of riding in the brand’s home in Routt County. The all-road bike is built around riding the paved roads and smooth “champagne gravel” that make up so much of the Steamboat Springs area.3

The Moots County Line will slot in between the Vamoots, the brand’s out-and-out road bike, and the Routt, the brand’s dedicated gravel bike that Moots updated earlier this year . Here are the details:

The County Line is Moot’s first true all-road bike, with the frame replacing the Vamoots 33 and clarifying the brand’s product line with three distinct drop bar bikes.

With 42mm of tire clearance, the County Line is similar to other endurance and all-road bikes that have been unveiled over the last year. The bike will sit between the clearance of the Trek Domane, with its 40mm of clearance, and the Allied Echo, which can run up to 45 mm tires.

Even though the bike fits up to 42mm, Moots has designed the bike around more moderate 38mm tires. To support 38mm tires, the bike is built with 425mm chainstays, a stable 70-73 degree head tube angle, and a 75mm bottom bracket drop. That low and long road geometry is built to support both road and light gravel riding, as the County Line walks the fine line between both ends of the drop bar spectrum.

Beyond the frame’s dimensions, the County Line brings a complete set of modern flourishes to the titanium frame. The County Line has an integrated front end with a custom titanium stem, a King i7 headset, and a D-shaped steerer tube. While the frame is titanium, like most high-end metal bikes, the County Line relies on the new carbon all-road fork to boost ride quality.

Speaking of ride quality, the frame is built with straight-gauge 3/2.5 titanium tubes, 1x and 2x compatibility, mounts for extra fenders and bottle cages, and a 45mm road chainline.

Moots has complete builds for the County Line with both 1x and 2x builds, although the frame is only compatible with fully wireless groupsets. Currently, the County Line is available in just the frameset spec. However, Moots has announced a lighter and stiffer RSL version of the frameset will be available in early 2027.

Consequently, complete bikes are built with both SRAM Force and Red XPLR and road groupset options. To finish the build, Moots uses a set of HED Vanquish 45 wheels and Vittoria Corsa Pro Control 38mm tires to offer a full slate of high-end all-road builds. Standalone framesets will start at $5,499 USD.

The new Moots Routt is available to order now. The premium RSL version will be available early in 2027. To learn more about the bike, visit the Moots website .

items.title: Silca Revives Cult Classic Omata Analog Bike Computer—But Only a Limited Number Can Be Made
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: The stylish, analog bike computer is back with the help of Silca, but getting one might prove to be a challenge.
items.lbText:
If you were into bikes around a decade ago, and specifically into bikes and on Instagram, you probably remember lusting after the Omata analog bike computer.

The circular, non-traditional computer looks more like a fine watch for your bike than a high performance tool (though it does a nice job of displaying the basics and tracking more data in the background for analyzing later).

The computer gained a lot of buzz and a cult following, but sadly the operation slowly faded over time.

Now, Silca , known for an ever growing number of luxury bike tools and components from pumps to chain wax to tires, has acquired Omata, bringing the bike computer back to production.

“At Silca, we are obsessed with the intersection of beauty, precision, and performance,” said Silca CEO Josh Poertner. “Omata is a masterpiece of functional art. We acquired Omata because we believed it was a product that should continue to exist in this world.”

Technically speaking, the device is a mechatronic cycling computer, meaning it combines a digital device with a mechanical display. It only displays speed, elapsed time, and elevation climbed, letting you access these key stats at a glance while riding, without bombarding you with page after page of stats and metrics. It’s like glancing at your wristwatch for the time instead of pulling out your phone and instantly getting distracted.

It’s not a device for athletes training for specific goals, doing intervals, or who want live power or heart rate figures. But fret not, that all-important data is captured in the background—including GPS data, heartrate, and power via ANT+ connection—so you can still share your ride with friends and track your stats in your training log. Ride files can be uploaded to your phone wirelessly via the iOS app (there’s no Android app unfortunately) or to your computer with a USB-C cable.

Silca’s involvement with Omate is deeper than just selling the computer. The brand has redesigned the internal circuit board, battery system, and outer housing while keeping the same form factor and analog display. The brand also redesigned the weather sealing, adding a “custom triple-barrier lip seal for the rotating bezel and a Gore-Tex membrane over the barometric pressure sensor for improved moisture resistance.”

For extra compatibility with existing computer mounts, Silca has updated the Omata with a square mounting cleat compatible with Garmin or Wahoo mounts.

If you want one, you won’t want to wait around to order, Silca is only selling a finite number. That’s not to keep the stock artificially low and the demand high, though. The number of devices that can ever be made is limited by the fact that it’s made with parts that are no longer being produced.

“Sadly, it relies on a finite supply of legacy Seiko components; so, each unit carries the weight of rarity,” Poertner said. “By bringing hand-assembly to our Indianapolis facility, we are ensuring each of these stunning instruments is tested for lasting performance.”

That, along with the premium alloy finish, rotating bezel, and unique interface of digital data tracking with an analog dial, also helps account for the lofty $800 price tag. That bests even Garmin’s priciest computer by $100, but no one is buying the Omata for pure performance reasons.

Silca will be making and releasing the computers in small batches until they’re sold out. The devices will be sold only in the U.S., though you might be able to have one sent internationally if you contact Silca directly; it never hurts to ask.

items.title: Rising US Racer Riley Sheehan Signs With Netcompany Ineos for Two Years
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: 'I still have so much more to achieve': Coloradan racer tapped up by former Tour de France dominator after shock exit of Filippo Ganna.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Filip Bezdek/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Riley Sheehan will spend the next two years of his budding pro career with Netcompany Ineos .

The Coloradan racer and his new team confirmed a two-year deal on Thursday, starting next season.

Sheehan is one of USA’s new generation of rising road racers.

Now aged 26, he became the first American to win the prestigious Paris-Tours one-day classic in what was then his trainee season in 2023.

This year, the powerful all-rounder won twice with his current team, NSN Cycling, and was called up to Team USA before Brandon McNulty won the recent road world championships.

“Joining the team is a dream come true,” Sheehan said Thursday. “It’s a team I’ve looked up to since I was young, and to now be part of such a successful and respected organization is incredibly special.

“I believe I still have so much more to achieve in my career, and having the backing of this team is the perfect next step for me,” he said.

“I’m excited to get started, set ambitious goals and give everything I have to help the team win, while continuing to push myself to become the best rider I can be.”

Sheehan came up through stalwart U.S. squads Aevolo and Rally, and spent a year on the NCL runaway league team.

He turned pro in 2024 and has been progressing since.

“Riley is an exciting rider. He’s fast, technically very skilled and has the ability to perform across a range of terrain,” said Netcompany Ineos head of racing Geraint Thomas.

“We see him being a great addition to our classics group, but he’s also a rider who can contribute right across the calendar,” Thomas said Thursday. “He brings plenty of versatility to the team, and we’re looking forward to helping him continue to develop.”

Sheehan is the latest in a flurry of new signings for Netcompany Ineos.

On Wednesday, the British team confirmed contracts with Clément Champoussin, James Shaw, and former Tour de l’Avenir winner Joseph Blackmore.

Spanish junior supertalent Benjamín Noval will also step directly to WorldTour with the team next year.

But it’s not been one-way traffic at Netcompany Ineos.

Marquee rider Filippo Ganna broke his contract this week to join Lidl-Trek.

The young American contingent of A.J. August, Artem Schmidt, and Magnus Sheffield are among a total of nine riders who will leave the team or retire this winter.

items.title: ‘A Dictatorship’: Team Picnic-PostNL Rocked by Allegations of Culture of Fear
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Dutch WorldTour team to open independent investigation into accounts of paranoia, distrust, and authoritarianism from dozens of former and current employees.
items.lbText:
Team Picnic-PostNL has promised to launch an independent investigation into shocking revelations unearthed by broadcaster NOS and the podcast In De Waaier.

The joint investigation by the two Dutch outlets exposed an atmosphere of fear, excessive control, and distrust that dates back more than a decade.

The project involved confidential interviews with 71 current and former Picnic-PostNL cycling team employees, and went live this week.

According to NOS , “many have terminated their employment traumatized. They speak of a ‘culture of fear’ and an ‘unsafe work situation.'”

The partnering men’s and women’s teams have seen superstar riders like Tom Dumoulin, Lorena Wiebes, and Romain Bardet on their books.

The embattled Picnic-PostNL team – which is currently dead last in both the men’s and women’s WorldTour rankings – rushed out a response Thursday.

The team said its offers to cooperate with the investigation by NOS and In De Waaier were ignored, and it promised “to commission an independent, professional investigation” into the allegations.

“In a performance-driven environment such as professional sport, things can go wrong. That is why there are several ways for people within our team to raise problems and concerns. Riders have a personal coach, there is a Rider Committee, and staff members can turn to confidential advisers. If people have felt unsafe within our organization or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened.

“We are proud of what we have built since 2008 together with the many people who are, or have been, part of and associated with this team. Precisely for that reason, we believe it is important to take a critical look at ourselves.

“We will therefore commission an independent, professional investigation into our team culture. We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may improvements, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL.”

Picnic-PostNL, formerly known as Team Giant, Sunweb, and DSM, has been stalked by rumors of a controlling, authoritarian culture for years.

Riders have broken contracts amid reports of burnout. Tales have emerged of riders being punished for adjusting their saddle height without authorization, and being forbidden from eating a kiwi.

One anonymous athlete once branded life at the team as a “Soviet regime.”

The long-read investigation published by NOS on Thursday is the most damning indictment of the team yet.

It detailed management taking constructive feedback as an attack on the team’s philosophy. Interviewees described a demeaning attitude toward riders and an unwillingness to flex plans to meet personal needs.

“It became a dictatorship,” said former coach Adriaan Helmantel, who worked with Giro d’Italia winner Dumoulin, amongst others.

In its statement Thursday, Picnic-PostNL outlined its values of safety, collaboration, and fairness, and rejected the claims made in NOS and In De Waaier .

“We do not recognize ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications,” reads the note.

“The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for.”

items.title: Doing Nothing Might Be Your Best Recovery Tool – and Now There’s Proof
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Rethink your recovery: Compression, cryotherapy, ice baths, and other costly tools fail to test better than doing nothing in new study.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Tim de Waele/Corbis via Getty Images)

Toss the compression socks, empty the ice bath, and cancel the recovery ride.

A new study has reinforced the theory that the best way to recover from a hard workout might be …. doing nothing.

No freezing cold-plunge. No $100 cryotherapy session. And definitely no compression socks.

A new study on endurance athletes suggests that sitting on the couch, eating well, and sleeping plenty might be just as effective as any costly, time-consuming recovery modality.

The researchers’ findings should have you rethink how you plan to recover from your next heinous interval session or gravel fondo.

Because while the study doesn’t definitively disprove certain recovery tools, it significantly questions the confidence of the claims used to sell them.

Investing time and money in compression socks, ice baths, cryotherapy sessions, and electrostim devices might be buying you little more than belief.

The premise that “you don’t overtrain, you under-recover” has driven an obsession with recovery hacks among cash-rich, time-poor amateurs who’re chasing easy gains.

Someone’s always selling a new “best way” to dodge DOMS, feel eternally fresh, and hit personal bests, every day.

What’s in the body, what’s in the mind? Was it the 10 hours of sleep or the four-minute cryotherapy session that saw you right after your most recent 100-mile ride?

Beyond that, the science behind many popular recovery tools rests on weak conclusions or is muddled by conflicts of interest.

A new independent paper published in August tries to cut through the noise.

By focusing on well-trained athletes who typically recover better than desk jockeys, it narrows the therapeutic window and reduces the chance for confounders. And unlike any previous review, it reports the certainty of its findings.

Take a breath before you read it: “ Physical recovery modalities in competitive and elite endurance athletes: a systematic review and network meta-analysis finding limited evidence of benefit over passive recovery .”

The study pooled trials of 273 “competitive, elite, or professional” cyclists, runners, swimmers, triathletes, and cross-country skiers. The mixed-sex cohort spanned a range of ages.

And don’t think the findings might not apply to you, dear reader. The minimum VO2 Max score required for inclusion was more than achievable for most athletes who “train” rather than tootle. These weren’t all Tour de France pros and Ironman champions.

Subjects were rated for DOMS (delayed onset muscle soreness), creatine kinase (a marker of muscle damage), performance restoration, and a number of other recovery markers after they used one or many popular recovery tools.

All the hip recovery modalities, and some old-school favorites, were put to the test.

The study focused on cold-water immersion, cryotherapy, neuromuscular electrical stimulation, massage, compression garments, and active recovery (i.e., an easy ride).

The comparators? Passive recovery (i.e., doing nothing) and, as a sham intervention, immersion in a room-temperature bath.

The experiment’s conclusion is bad news for your trusty compression socks. It doesn’t do much for the burgeoning recovery technology industry, either.

The headline? No recovery tool can claim to be better than doing nothing.

“In competitive and elite endurance athletes, no physical recovery modality has been shown to outperform passive recovery on any outcome we examined,” reads the summary.

“For sport-specific performance, the evidence goes further: compression garments, active recovery, and neuromuscular electrical stimulation can be said, with low to moderate certainty, not to produce a clinically important benefit.”

The study also failed to find any comparative benefit of one recovery method over another. A $100 cryotherapy session might be no better than a 30-minute recovery ride.

But that said, this isn’t the brink of armageddon for ice baths, compression socks, or Ridley Scott-inspired cryotherapy chambers.

The study’s findings are far from conclusive, despite using 47 comparison trials across nearly 300 athletes.

The authors themselves point out several weaknesses in the methodology and complicating factors in the interpretation of the results. Indeed, result certainty was rated “very low” in 31 of the 47 trials comparing a recovery tool vs. doing nothing.

The one “moderate-certainty” finding might raise eyebrows, however. It might also reduce the average sock height in the finishing area of your next gran fondo or post-race flight.

The evidence concluded with reasonable certainty that compression garments – the cheapest, easiest, most accessible recovery modality out there – do not improve performance.

Recovery, however, is not all in the legs.

The placebo effect of any recovery modality is strong.

That’s why, in the science-backed Tour de France, you still see riders shivering in ice baths after a stage and staggering around hotels squeezed into compression socks.

As Tudor Pro Cycling trainer James Spragg once told Velo :

“Some of the things riders use in recovery could also be considered placebos, or aren’t so well-proven. But to be honest, we don’t care if some things in the recovery protocol ‘work’ or not, just as long as riders feel it’s a benefit,” Spragg said.

“If a rider feels more confident for the next day as a result of something in their recovery process, it’s all a benefit,” he added.

As Spragg said, belief is a powerful component of recovery, as it is of performance.

Many studies have found that recovery methods with the most noticeable sensory effect typically have the strongest influence on reported outcomes.

For example, the pressure of a compression sock or the shock of an ice bath might convince athletes they’re primed for PRs in their next workout.

The new paper reinforces the placebo theory by using a room temperature bath as a “sham” intervention.…

items.title: No Medal Ride for Taylor Phinney as USA Team Pursuit Starts Road to LA 2028
items.author: ahood
items.content: Phinney is back. Team USA takes seventh at track worlds as the fight for eight LA28 team pursuit spots begins.
items.lbText:
Phinney, right, competed in track worlds in China. (Photo: Sean M. Haffey/Getty Image)

Taylor Phinney ’s return to the track ended short of the medal rounds Wednesday as Team USA finished seventh in the men’s team pursuit in the Shanghai UCI Track Cycling World Championships .

But all is not lost as the team opens a long, 18-month fight to earn one of eight qualifying spots for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games .

Phinney, newly crowned U23 road world champion Ashlin Barry , Grant Koontz and Anders Johnson clocked 3:50.916 in the second leg of racing.

The Americans led early against France but lost their heat by 1.297 seconds, posting the seventh-fastest time among the eight teams.

France advanced to Thursday’s bronze-medal final against Great Britain. Denmark and Italy will race for gold.

The Americans squeezed into the first round with a qualifying time of 3:51.029, finishing seventh among 18 nations and 6.038 seconds behind defending champion Denmark.

They shaved just over a tenth of a second off that mark in their second ride, while France found nearly two seconds to advance.

Also Wednesday, Team USA’s women’s team pursuit — racing without heavy hitters like Chloé Dygert and Jennifer Valente — stopped the clock in ninth, and missed qualifying for the medal rounds on Thursday.

Team USA and Phinney were hoping for more in one of the biggest American cycling’s biggest comeback stories this season .

For Phinney, a two-time individual pursuit world champion, Shanghai marked his first worlds since coming out of retirement to chase a spot at the home Olympics.

“This is my first race back. It feels good, it feels like coming home. It’s fun riding with the guys,” Phinney said before racing.

“We have a really strong team, but it’s a question mark coming into the race to understand where the other teams are at. If we can do a top 5, we’d be happy with that,” he said. “We will take it one round at a time”

The result fell short of that ambition and of the benchmark the American program set last year, when the squad was fourth in the 2025 worlds.

Team USA’s last worlds medals in team pursuit was bronze way back in 1995.

Phinney, 36, returns to a discipline that also looks radically different from when he raced in the 2008 Olympic Games in track.

“The technology has changed quite a lot, especially in team pursuit. If you look at my (body) position in the individual pursuit, it was completely wide open, and now everything is super closed,” he said. “I think the position is more extreme, but the power numbers, they’re not, like, so much different.”

Team USA’s men’s squad has a big mountain to climb to qualify for the Olympic Games.

While the women’s team pursuit won gold in Paris 2024 , the men didn’t even field a team and has never won an Olympic medal in team pursuit.

Phinney and rising star Barry give the squad new hope, but it won’t be easy.

Only eight nations per gender will qualify for the LA28 for team pursuit and the road to Los Angeles started Wednesday. The points window runs from this week at the Shanghai worlds through April 2028.

Seventh at these worlds provides an early marker to build on, but it’s far from guaranteeing a spot in Los Angeles.

Team USA will need to keep scoring against the same deep field across the qualifying World Cups, Pan American championships, and next year’s track worlds.

The next qualifying event to watch is the World Cup series, which starts April 2-4, 2027, in Milton, Canada. That’s followed by Hong Kong on April 23-25 and another Chinese round from April 30 to May 2.

The 2027 world championships provide another major test, with the track competition scheduled for August 26-30 at Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines as part of the “super worlds” set for France next summer.

For Phinney and the Americans, the first race is in the books.

Now comes the hard part of competing against the confirmed power houses like Denmark, Great Britain, Australia, and Italy, and finish inside the top eight to punch their ticket to Los Angeles.

items.title: Why Anyone Would Pay $6,500 for Great Wheels When $1,399 Gets You Really Close
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: When Chinese brands like Elitewheels give you good performance for a fraction of the cost of the most expensive wheelsets, what exactly is a luxury brand actually selling you?
items.lbText:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

When Tom Pidcock showed up at the UCI Road World Championships riding a set of wheels with a bright white logo that few people had seen and even fewer had ridden, everyone started talking. Those in the industry knew the logo, though. I’d had long conversations with the brand, Partington, a year earlier about those exact wheels, and I knew right away that they were both exceptionally expensive and very rare.

Mostly though, those $6,500 Partington R-Series Performance Ti wheels got me thinking. In a moment when you can get great wheels for about 1/5th that price with specs that almost match, the Partingtons are a beacon. They don’t just represent genius engineering—although they are impressive on that front. They represent next-level marketing. Those wheels showing up under Pidcock at Worlds are a blueprint for how Western brands are still able to compete even when the pricing floor disappears.

The Partington R-Series Performance Ti in the 65mm depth is likely the wheelset Pidcock was on. There’s a possibility it’s the 50mm version (we weren’t able to get up close and personal with Pidcock’s bike to confirm), but for the sake of this article I’m focusing on the 65. I find it a more interesting wheel anyway. It’s 65mm deep with a sealed rim bed, a 23mm internal width, a 34mm external width, and a weight of 1,265 grams.

Just to be clear: those are absurdly impressive specs. Only a handful of wheels exist with anything close, and I’m not sure any quite match it across the board. The already high-end Zipp 454 NSW would have been the natural alternative—since he races on Zipp wheels for his Pinarello-Q 36.5 trade team—but it is shallower and about 100 grams heavier.

As for how they ride, I may get the chance to tell you firsthand in the future. For now, it’s irrelevant to the point I’m making. Assume the wheelset rides well—I’m certain it does, and it damn well better for $6,500.

You know what else likely rides well, though? The Elitewheels Drive SL 58D CS for $1,399. That wheelset has a 25mm internal width, a 36mm front / 34mm rear external width, a 58mm depth, and weighs 1,330 grams. Granted, you’ll probably have to tape the rim bed yourself. But at that price, you can wipe off the excess sealant with a hundred-dollar bill and still be well ahead.

And Elitewheels is just one of many Chinese brands making competitive wheelsets, frames, and components at a fraction of the cost of Western brands.

This is where I see things getting really interesting. When you look at the Elitewheels website, the marketing is, compared to Western brands, a bit bare bones. The Drive SL wheelset is shown as a 3D render on a generic black background. There are a couple of views, but they are essentially the same aside from a measurement drawing. There’s no aspirational images of riders using the wheels in the Swiss Alps, or wheels in a high-tech testing facility.

At Partington, you are greeted with an entirely different approach. You’ve probably already seen the wheels being used by Pidcock on the biggest stage in road racing, signifying the brand’s performance credentials. Then when you visit the website, you first see an image of a rider in a beautiful setting, actual images of the wheels, and an in-depth explanation and backstory about what sets the wheels apart.

Both wheelsets use carbon spokes, but whereas Elitewheels has nothing more to say about its spokes, the Partington wheels use “FLEXON” carbon spokes with a description about the kind of carbon they’re made of. Then there is the hub. Both are titanium, but the Elitewheels hub is simply a “one-piece titanium freehub” that “delivers instant engagement.” The Partington hub? That is a “PERFORM hub” engineered “using detailed Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to refine structural geometry, reduce mass while maintaining stiffness and ensuring efficient load transfer in real world conditions.” That sounds very special, right? Except every major manufacturer uses FEA.

Or maybe you really want to know about the details of the packaging. Don’t worry, Partington has you covered: “Wheels are packed individually in lithographically printed telescope-style boxes featuring a matte cellophane finish with spot UV varnish. Each wheel is held securely in a vacuum‑molded insert.” As someone who spent a decade as a print designer, I know exactly what that means. To most people, it is a completely irrelevant detail described in the most technical way possible. You either pretend you know what it is or simply believe it must be incredibly special. Elitewheels does not tell you about the packaging, in case you were wondering.

None of this is a bad thing, and the point here isn’t to drag Partington. The R-Series wheels genuinely represent incredible engineering with tangible differences from the competition.

Instead, the point is that Partington is walking the fine line of luxury performance. The brand is selling you on the idea of incredible performance in the exact same way Lamborghini does. It’s likely not performance you need (a Toyota can hit the speed limit all the same), and it might not even be performance everyday riders like you and me can realistically feel compared to the competition (again, I’ll see when I finally ride them), but the conversation has to start with performance.

That performance is only the foundation, though. Once it’s established, it’s time for the heritage and craftsman story to take over. You aren’t just buying a wheel from a factory brand like Zipp (never mind that those wheels are hand-built, too); you are buying an artisan product from a visionary founder manufacturing in Australia. Sure, it’s a highly technical bike wheel, but it’s also functional art, and that is the key.…

items.title: Tour de France Boss Rejects Radical Idea to Cut Race to Two Weeks
items.author: ahood
items.content: Reducing the grand tours to make way for the UCI calendar reforms? Prudhomme defends the Tour’s format, and the Giro and Vuelta bosses aren’t giving up race days either.
items.lbText:
Christian Prudhomme, far left, pushed back against the idea of shortening the Tour de France. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Shrinking the Tour de France and the other grand tours to make room for the UCI ‘s controversial cycling overhaul?

No way, says Tour boss Christian Prudhomme.

“The Tour de France lasts three weeks, four weekends, and that’s perfectly fine,” Prudhomme told RMC Sport .

Prudhomme said he’s not interested in trimming cycling’s biggest race as proposals to shorten grand tours have kick-started a larger debate over the sport’s crowded calendar.

Speaking just days ahead of the unveiling of the 2027 Tour route, the Tour director defended its current format.

“That question concerns certain grand tours,” he said.

If the Tour vetoes any attempt to tweak the three-week format that dates back to its founding, that leaves the Giro d’Italia and Vuelta a España squarely on the chopping block.

But the bosses of cycling’s other grand tours aren’t buying into the idea to lose a weekend, either.

The debate comes as the UCI maps out potential reforms to professional cycling that could be rolled out by as soon as 2029.

Its “ Agenda 2030 ” consultation drew 55 submissions from teams, riders, organizers, federations, sponsors, manufacturers, and broadcasters.

Unveiled during the Montréal road worlds, the outline covers a broad range of issues that are on the table, including the calendar, cycling’s economic model, fan engagement, rider safety , and the integrity of results via doping controls .

Other ideas include a budget cap, sharing some commercial revenues, and improving broadcasting and marketing to reach today’s social-media savvy audience.

The UCI has since appointed Deloitte as a strategic adviser and the initial reform proposals are due to be presented in December, with the first measures potentially arriving in 2029.

One ideal outcome for backers of shorter grand tours is that the biggest stars like Tadej Pogačar, Jonas Vingegaard, and Remco Evenepoel might race all three rather than just obsessing on the Tour.

Right now, everything is on the table, and no firm proposals have been made.

But one of the most contentious ideas is to squeeze the grand tours into three weekends instead of four.

Some are floating the idea of shortening the Giro and Vuelta to 16 or 17 days, but keeping the Tour at 21 stages.

That idea is not without its supporters.

Some see the Giro and Vuelta dragging on too long sometimes, and the argument is that those extra days could free up some space on the calendar and help some races like Paris-Nice and Tirreno-Adriatico from overlapping.

The other grand tour bosses are having none of it.

New Giro director Luca Guercilena pushed back during an interview with Domestique at Il Lombardia.

“Grand tours must remain grand tours and the Giro d’Italia isn’t going to change. All three grand tours must be the same length,” the Italian said. “There can be no differences.”

The three-week grand tour format is one that grew organically over time. The first Tour in 1903 stretched across 19 days with just six monster stages averaging more than 400km, separated by rest days.

The Giro and later the Vuelta followed, and the grand tours settled into the now-familiar 21-stage, three-week rhythm.

For Guercilena, the brutal third week is the essential ingredient to what decides a grand tour winner.

“Cycling is an endurance sport, and it’s over three weeks that you can truly see if athletes are endurance riders,” he told RMC Sport . “We have no intention of changing that. I understand the UCI and its president, David Lappartient, who believe that overlapping races aren’t good for anyone. But the grand tours must remain three weeks long.”

Vuelta director Javier Guillén drew an equally firm line in a recent interview with MARCA .

“We are not in favor of eliminating any days, not even one. It’s true that the debate is ongoing, but at this time, it is not being discussed at any official or institutional level,” Guillén said.

The Giro and Vuelta have long defended their place alongside the Tour, and resisted any efforts to reduce the number of race days.

Of course, race organizers have a vested interest because every race day comes with lucrative host city start and finish fees, TV rights revenue, and fees from the publicity caravan.

“We believe that the days honoring the great icons of cycling should remain untouched, because otherwise we would all be worse off,” Guillén told the Spanish daily. “There’s no point in doing that.”

The Vuelta moved from April to September and now August in 1995, and the new place on the calendar has helped the Spanish grand tour grow in stature.

For 2027, however, the Vuelta will be contested after the UCI Road World Championships for the first time since the switch to make room for the second edition of “super worlds.”

items.title: Anti-Doping Agency Defends Testing Cyclist Same Day Her Mom Died
items.author: ahood
items.content: The ITA says testers were unaware of Cavallar’s mother's death before arriving for anti-doping control and confirms it apologized.
items.lbText:
The ITA said it reached out to Valentina Cavallar following an anti-doping control on the same day her mother died. (Photo: Tommaso Berardi/NurPhoto)

The International Testing Agency defended its decision to complete a doping control at Valentina Cavallar ’s home shortly after her mother died, but added that it had apologized to the Austrian rider.

Responding to questions from Velo , the ITA said neither the agency nor the doping control officer knew about the death before the officer arrived for an out-of-competition control on September 5.

According to the ITA, the officer learned of her mother’s passing only upon arriving at the door. Cavallar and her family cooperated with the procedure and did not ask for it to be postponed or stopped.

“Faced with an exceptionally sensitive situation, the DCO, with the rider and her family’s support, endeavoured to pursue the procedure as discreetly, respectfully and swiftly as possible,” the ITA said.

The response follows Cavallar’s emotional account of undergoing the surprise doping control in a room next to where her mother’s body lay.

The 25-year-old SD Worx-Protime climber revealed the incident on a post on Instagram and also explained why she ended her season early after the Tour de France Femmes .

“What made this experience even harder was that just a few hours after my mum had passed away, I had to undergo a doping control at home, in the room next to where she lay,” Cavallar wrote.

Cavallar’s incident appears to be an extraordinary coincidence.

Riders must report their whereabouts and designate a daily 60-minute window when they are available for controls, though testers can also arrive unannounced at any time.

In an earlier story by Velo’s Andy McGrath , riders recalled getting caught out by wedding plans, broken-down cars, and an all-night bender that left one rider away from home when testers arrived at 6 a.m.

Cavallar said she understood her obligations as a professional athlete, but questioned having to do the test in the middle of a family crisis.

“But in that moment, I was clearly not thinking about cycling, competition or my responsibilities as an athlete. I was a daughter who had just lost her mum,” she wrote.

The ITA — which runs cycling’s anti-doping program — said it investigated the circumstances after learning of her post and contacted her directly.

“We fully recognize that undergoing a doping control in these circumstances has added to her distress experienced at an extraordinarily painful time. We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologized,” ITA said.

The agency also encouraged athletes to raise concerns during or after controls so it could balance anti-doping requirements with their privacy and wellbeing.

The International Testing Agency (ITA) extends its sincere condolences to Valentina Cavallar and her family following the loss of her mother.

Since learning about the circumstances of the sample collection which took place on 5 September 2026 on Valentina Cavallar, the ITA looked into the context of the test.

Neither the ITA nor the Doping Control Officer (DCO) were aware of the rider’s personal situation prior to arriving at her home. The DCO was informed of her mother’s passing upon arrival. According to the information gathered by the ITA since the rider’s Instagram post [Monday], Ms Cavallar and her family cooperated fully with the procedure, and no concerns or requests to postpone or discontinue the control were raised at the time or afterwards.

Faced with an exceptionally sensitive situation, the DCO, with the rider and her family’s support, endeavoured to pursue the procedure as discreetly, respectfully and swiftly as possible.

We fully recognise that undergoing a doping control in these circumstances has added to her distress experienced at an extraordinarily painful time. We have been in touch with the rider directly and apologised.

The ITA remains committed to ensuring that the protection of clean sport goes hand in hand with respect, compassion and care for athletes.

We will also continue to always encourage athletes to report any concerns either during or after a doping control, so the ITA can take the appropriate measures to ensure a proportionate balance between the fight against doping and every athlete’s right to privacy and wellbeing.

items.title: Sprint Ace Richardson Breaks Silence After Being Booted from China Track Worlds for Alleged Discrimination
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Matthew Richardson vows to co-operate 'with contrition' in misconduct investigation after being sent home from track world championships.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Dilara Irem Sancar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Matthew Richardson has promised to cooperate “with contrition” in investigations over his alleged discrimination and misconduct.

On Monday, the 27-year-old sprinter was booted from the British team for this week’s track world championships in Shanghai following allegations made against him , including by other athletes.

According to The Times , Richardson was found “making discriminatory remarks about people from minority backgrounds and even joking about his use of the N-word.”

British Cycling has opened an internal investigation into Richardson’s conduct. The rider was sent home from China earlier this week.

Richardson responded to the allegations for the first time Tuesday via a post on Instagram .

“I understand the seriousness of what has been raised in recent reports about my withdrawal from the 2026 UCI Track Cycling World Championships,” he wrote.

“British Cycling has said it looks into matters like this through its established procedures. I will co-operate fully with its processes. I assure everyone that I will do so properly, and appropriately and with contrition for the feelings of anyone who might be affected.

“Out of fairness to everyone involved, and on advice, like British Cycling, I will not be commenting further until any process is complete. I am deeply disappointed to miss the World Championships, and I wish the Great Britain team and every rider competing the very best.

“I ask that my family’s privacy is respected at this time.”

Richardson locked the comments section on his post.

Richardson’s shock ejection from the British team reshaped the narrative going into track worlds.

The sprint powerhouse was seen as a stone-cold lock for medals at the team sprint, sprint and keirin events.

Richardson’s major rival Harry Lavreysen told De Telegraaf he’d miss the competition. The Dutchman was beaten by Richardson to the European sprint and keirin titles earlier this season.

“I’m eager for a rematch,” Lavreysen said Tuesday. “Richardson was also in Japan [where Lavreysen trained last summer, ed.], and when I saw him riding there with those European stripes and stars on his jersey, it really got to me.

“I wasn’t in my best shape in February, but I am now,” Lavreysen said. “So I would have loved to beat him here.”

The UCI track world championships run October 14-18.

items.title: You Can’t Ride That Bike in the Dirt
items.author: Kelly Matkovich
items.content: Sixteen years of Belgian Waffle Ride suggest otherwise. Registration for the 2027 season opens October 13, with desert adventures, high-country escapes and plenty to celebrate after the finish.
items.lbText:
Riders moving in a dirt sector at Belgian Waffle Ride Utah. (Photo: Belgian Waffle Ride)

The road bike was supposed to stay on the road. Michael Marckx was supposed to get to school on time. Somewhere between those two expectations, a dirt shortcut presented itself.

He pointed his bike down a series of whoops and across a field, passing a group of older kids who apparently had strong opinions about where bicycles belonged. “You can’t ride that bike in the dirt,” one yelled.

“I had just done it, so the argument seemed weak,” Marckx writes in his manuscript, You Can’t Ride That Bike in the Dirt . The exchange stayed with him, along with a fascination for the battered riders and cobbled roads of Paris-Roubaix, his family’s Flemish heritage, and the waffles that followed long days of running and riding. Decades later, those ingredients found their way into a Southern California bicycle event with an unusually hospitable name.

The Belgian Waffle Ride sounded like breakfast. The course suggested someone had forgotten to mention a few things.

In 2012, riders gathered over waffles and coffee before heading into a long day of pavement, dirt, climbing and sand. They returned to food, Lost Abbey ale and stories that could only have come from spending hours trying to hold themselves and their bicycles together. The arrangement proved enduring: feed people, take them somewhere extraordinary, ask more of them than they expected, and give them a place to celebrate afterward.

In 2027, Belgian Waffle Ride enters its 16th year with events in Arizona, California, Utah, Montana and Mexico, plus another destination in development. Registration opens Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at 8 a.m. Pacific , inviting riders to start planning where next year’s stories will happen.

On the course, the appeal becomes clear somewhere around the first change of surface. A smooth stretch of pavement lets a group find its rhythm, wheels humming and conversations returning. Then the road gives way to dirt. Riders spread out, look ahead and choose their lines. Someone who was working hard to stay attached on the road suddenly looks comfortable. Someone else discovers that fitness and handling are separate subjects.

Marckx and co-founder Phil Tinstman built that uncertainty into BWR. Each surface creates possibilities, and each equipment choice carries a compromise. Fast tires have their virtues until the sand arrives. A comfortable bike on rough ground may ask more of its rider on the pavement. Pacing, fueling and the ability to adapt become as useful as a big engine.

In his manuscript, Marckx describes the original course as “an interrogation of the whole cyclist.” Over the years, that idea has become Unroad: riding that follows the character of a place across whichever surfaces make the journey interesting.

It also leaves room for different kinds of riders. Professionals may be settling the race at the front while friends farther back are helping one another through a difficult sector. A first-time participant can be discovering the pleasure of riding beyond familiar roads while an experienced racer is discovering the limits of an overly confident tire choice.

The established Waffle, Wafer and Wanna distances offer different portions of that experience. The full Waffle asks for a substantial day; the middle-distance Wafer and shorter Wanna give riders other ways to explore the terrain and challenge themselves. Each leads back to the gathering that made breakfast worth getting up for in the first place.

The 2027 journey begins in the Sonoran Desert, Arizona, March 5–6 , with the fifth annual Hell of the North Desert. Sandy washes, twisting trails and open gravel give the landscape a rhythm of its own. The desert rewards attention: carry momentum here, choose a line there, save enough for whatever comes around the next bend. Between efforts, there is the pleasure of looking up and remembering why a bicycle was worth bringing to this place. Waffle, Wafer and Wanna options let riders choose how much desert they want in their day.

By May 1–2 , the community returns to San Diego County for the 16th BWR California , the Hell of the North County. This is where the original idea took root, and the changing terrain still supplies its personality. Pavement connects sandy and rocky sectors; climbs separate groups that seemed perfectly cooperative a few minutes earlier. The course keeps asking riders to change gears in every sense of the phrase. California’s weekend also includes the Gran Roadie-Oh for those drawn to a paved adventure, with its 2027 details to follow.

Two weeks later, Cedar City, Utah, hosts BWR May 14–15 . The eighth annual event, presented by BZI, moves into May and returns riders to long gravel sectors, open high-desert views and riding at altitude. Here, the distance can unfold slowly across an enormous landscape, making restraint early in the day a useful investment. Utah is also preparing for substantial changes in 2027. A fuller announcement is coming soon; for now, the new date marks the beginning of an exciting chapter for the Hell of the South West.

There may soon be another place to point the bike. Organizers are excited about adding an event in the middle of the country, potentially in July . The location, timing and course are still coming together, with details to follow as plans are finalized.

The season then reaches Bozeman, Montana, September 17–18 , for the third Hell of the Bozone. Broad valleys, rolling ranchlands, gravel climbs and backcountry terrain give the riding a generous sense of scale. Fast stretches invite an effort; rougher ground asks riders to leave something in reserve. Moving into a late-season weekend gives participants a new reason to make a trip of it, with time to enjoy Bozeman after the bike has been leaned against something sturdy.…

items.title: Who Won and Lost Most in 2026? Pogačar Crushed Then Crashed, and Picnic Has Big Problems
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Year-end victory and UCI points rankings: 5 key takes, including moneyball tactics, no-filler seasons, and a brutal tale of haves and have-nots.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Florian Wiegand/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Tadej Pogačar doesn’t need a full season to dominate, Picnic-PostNL needs a rescue package, and moneyball tactics pay off.

They’re some of the top takeaways from the individual and team rankings in this final week of 2026.

Il Lombardia wrapped up all the major racing on the 2026 calendar last weekend, and the individual victory and UCI points rankings are all but set.

They tell some interesting tales of haves, have-nots, breakouts and busts.

Summary tables for the peloton’s top-20 riders and all 18 WorldTour teams can be found below, with splits for victories and UCI points.

These are not expected to change significantly as the season winds down with low-key races through Europe and Asia before it comes to a full stop this Sunday.

Here are five of the most eye-catching takeaways from the end-of-year leagues.

Tadej Pogačar didn’t even need a full season to obliterate everybody this year. The 28-year-old topped the victory and UCI rankings by several bike lengths, despite his season starting late at Strade Bianche and ending abruptly on August 29.

Pogi won 22 times this year and scored eight more victories next-best rider Paul Magnier.

Super-prestige victories at the Tour de France, two WorldTour stage races, Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and Strade Bianche saw Pogačar dominate the UCI points rankings in just 45 race days.

His individual 9,000-point haul from six months matched or exceeded what four entire teams could manage all year. It was more than three times what 30 riders could pick off at poor Picnic-PostNL.

Second-place Remco Evenepoel was choking on Pogi’s exhaust, 2,000 UCI points back.

It’s almost scary to consider what Pogačar could have achieved this year.

The GOAT could have finished 2026 with more than 12,000 UCI points if a brutal crash at the Vuelta a España hadn’t denied him the red jersey and the chance to fulfill the role as favorite for the world championships, European champs, and Il Lombardia.

For context, Pogačar scored 11,655 points in his Hall of Fame 2024 season.

A very tepid take? Pogačar will top the victory and points leagues again in 2027. The only question is by how far.

UAE Emirates-XRG was the winningest team of 2026, but this was a long way from its absolute rout of 2025.

The team of Tadej Pogačar, Isaac del Toro and world champion Brandon McNulty “only” won 77 times this year. That’s a long way short of the single-season win record of 95 it set last year, and its worst return since 2023.

It’s a luxury letdown for UAE Emirates-XRG.

Despite dropping 18 wins year-on-year, it remains in its own tier of the WorldTour. The state-backed superteam towers over its rival Visma-Lease a Bike and Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, who won 51 and 42 times, respectively.

So what went “wrong” for the world’s richest, deepest team in 2026?

1. João Almeida won nothing. Zilch. The Portuguese star won 10 times last year but failed to get off the mark in his illness-riddled annus horribilis.

2. Juan Ayuso left. The Spaniard won seven times for UAE Emirates-XRG last year, despite a spicy spat with management. Those victories weren’t replaced.

3. As we wrote above, Pogačar lost the chance to bank a hatful of late-season wins after he was upended at the Vuelta.

Bettering brilliance, it’s a tough job to have.

The 2026 rankings are a brutal tale of haves and have-nots.

While UAE Emirates-XRG is miles off the front, Picnic-PostNL is so far off the pace it would need multiple sticky bottles to catch up.

Picnic-PostNL won only two times this year and collected just 2,680 points.

Of the WorldTour teams, it’s dead last in the UCI points league. Beyond that, it’s been outscored by 10 lower-tier rivals in a full UCI ranking that includes ProTeams and Conti teams.

And it could have been even worse . The disaster Dutch team was stuck on just one victory until Pavel Bittner snatched sprint victory and allowed a brief flush of pride this September at Paris-Chauny.

The bad news – Bittner, the team’s brightest prospect, is leaving for Pinarello-Q36.5.

Picnic-PostNL is facing an existential crisis right now.

The squad recently denied reports it was contemplating relegating itself to the second-tier of racing for 2027, but the writing seems to be on the wall.

Money in Sport reported in January that the team has lost €19.5m over three years. Bike sponsor Lapierre is fighting for survival. Bittner’s exit, along with the departure of former winners Fabio Jakobsen and Casper van Uden, suggests the team will be fighting for survival next year, too.

The partnering women’s team is in similar trouble. It hasn’t put a single “W” in the column all year.

Picnic-PostNL should maybe consult XDS-Astana for some tips.

The Kazakh crew punched way above its mid-tier budget to land sixth in both the victory and UCI rankings for 2026.

But how does a team without one of the peloton’s “bigs” collect 32 wins and 16,028 points?! It outperformed Lidl-Trek, Soudal Quick-Step, and Alpecin-Premier Tech, all without a Tim Merlier, a Mads Pedersen, or an MVDP.

XDS-Astana reprised its points-farming policies of 2025 with wild success in 2026.

Winningest rider Matteo Malucelli took eight of his nine victories for the year by bullying lower-tier rivals in a month of late-season racing across Asia. Likewise, Christian Scaroni gobbled top-10s in all the one-day and stage races nobody else bothered to show up to.

But to give the team its due – Guillermo Silva finished 14th in the win rankings courtesy of one of the year’s breakout seasons. When he wasn’t scoring “easy wins” at 2.pro stage races, the 24-year-old won a stage, wore the pink jersey, and finished in the top-6 four times at the Giro d’Italia.

XDS-Astana gets heat for its data-driven, distinctly unglamorous approach to rider scheduling.

It’s not pretty, but it works damn well.…

items.title: Visma-Lease a Bike Signs Belgian Teenager With Eye on Post-Vingegaard Era
items.author: ahood
items.content: Visma signs Belgian prospect Seff Van Kerckhove through 2030 with hopes of developing its next Tour de France champion in latest superteam talent quest.
items.lbText:
Seff Van Kerckhove won bronze in the world time trial race in Rwanda in 2025. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Visma-Lease a Bike is already building for the post- Jonas Vingegaard era and penned one of Belgium’s most hyped young talents to a long-term deal through 2030.

Seff Van Kerckhove , 18, will join the Dutch superteam’s development squad next season, with a possible fast track to the WorldTour in the works.

Hyped as a potential grand tour talent, the 18-year-old is seen by some as the Belgian prince to Remco Evenepoel . He won 11 races across 2026, including time trials and mountain stages on the European junior racing circuit.

Visma’s development boss sounds keen to give him some breathing room as the Dutch team looks to the future .

“He has shown a strong commitment to his development, and we believe he has the mindset and qualities needed to continue progressing,” said Visma head of development Robbert de Groot. “We believe Seff has the qualities to take significant steps forward over the long term.”

Van Kerckhove missed last month’s worlds in Montréal after a driver struck him during training . Visma said he is recovering well.

He will join newly crowned U23 world champion Ashlin Barry on a development squad that is hardly short of ambition.

The move also takes him out of Decathlon’s orbit. Van Kerckhove raced for its U19 squad, but will head to Visma rather than continue along the French team’s pathway toward a possible future alongside Paul Seixas .

There is a family connection waiting for him, too. Older brother Matisse Van Kerckhove, 20, will graduate to Visma’s WorldTour roster in 2027.

“It is a great honor to join one of the biggest teams in cycling,” Van Kerckhove said. “I believe in the team’s sporting project and am convinced that it offers the ideal environment for me to continue developing and get the best out of myself.”

The signing is another move in the increasingly high-stakes scramble among the WorldTour superteams to secure cycling’s next generation before someone else does.

Riders like Evenepoel, Seixas, and Isaac del Toro have proven that young riders barely out their teens can produce huge results in the WorldTour.

Every team is scrambling to find that next diamond-in-the-rough.

Netcompany-Ineos landed Spanish junior prodigy Benjamín Noval , 18, to join its WorldTour roster in 2027. The son of the former pro of the same name dominated junior stage races, and won double gold at the Montréal junior worlds .

Netcompany-Ineos also signed Patrik Pezzo Rosola — son of Olympic mountain champion Paola Pezzo — to its junior squad for 2027.

Lorenzo Finn , 19, heads to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe’s WorldTour team in 2027 after winning the Baby Giro and Tour de l’Avenir in 2026.

Another Spanish gem in Héctor Álvarez Martínez, also 19, steps up at Lidl-Trek after two seasons on its development team, a European title, and second place at the U23 worlds.

Most of the major WorldTour teams already fund their own U23 and junior development squads. Otherwise they risk being left behind.

UAE Team Emirates Gen Z will promote Davide Stella — who suffered a brutal high-speed crash at the AlUla Tour — to the WorldTour squad in 2027.

Visma has spent the past half decade building out its development operation that’s already delivering riders who can win straight away.

Per Strand Hagenes is the latest payoff. The Norwegian joined the development squad in 2022, moved to the WorldTour in 2024, and broke through in 2026 with two victories, including Sunday’s Paris-Tours, and second at E3 Saxo Classic.

Matthew Brennan is another Visma development product who enjoyed a blowout 2026. In his second full WorldTour season, the Briton won 12 races, including Kuurne-Brussels-Kuurne and five stages at the Vuelta a España .

Finding the next Vingegaard won’t be easy. Tour de France-caliber riders are the rarest of talents .

The Dane remains under contract through 2028 and turns 30 in December. With two Tour de France titles and victories at the Giro and Vuelta, he’s been at the center of Visma’s grand tour success this entire decade.

There have been unsubstantiated rumors that Vingegaard might want to end his career at Uno-X, the Danish-Norwegian outfit that recently signed Magnus Sheffield as its first American rider .

Van Kerckhove’s signing shows that Visma is clearly thinking about what comes next, even if the team’s sponsorship future remains unconfirmed and after some high-profile backroom reshuffles .

Visma still packs 2023 Vuelta winner Sepp Kuss, Matteo Jorgenson , and rising Italian Davide Piganzoli to carry its ambitions alongside Vingegaard .

Piganzoli, 24, won five races in 2026, finished eighth leading at the Giro, and hit 14th in his Tour debut.

Visma is already moving its chess pieces to stay at the top of the game.
